analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal tax on individuals' capital gains from selling investments.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in the House Ways and Means Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed capital gains from taxable income for individuals and other non-corporate taxpayers, meaning profits from selling stocks, real estate, or other assets would be tax-free starting in 2002. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which took no action on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who sell capital assets — stocks, bonds, real estate, businesses. Capital gains are heavily concentrated among the highest-income households, so the largest dollar benefit would go to wealthy investors. The bill's title frames the cut as encouraging investment and job creation.

how_it_helps.text: Excludes net capital gain from gross income for all taxpayers other than corporations, so individuals would pay no federal income tax on profits from selling capital assets [S2][S3].
Repeals the existing special capital gains rate structure (striking the rate provisions) and makes the exclusion effective for tax years beginning after 2001 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately everyone who relies on federal programs or pays other taxes, because revenue from capital gains — a tax source that falls mostly on high-income households — would disappear.

drawbacks.text: The exclusion would eliminate federal tax on investment profits for all non-corporate taxpayers, a tax source that falls disproportionately on the highest-income households, shifting the cost of government onto wages and other taxes [S2][S3].
The Treasury would forgo substantial revenue, adding pressure on the federal deficit or forcing other tax increases or spending cuts, with the bill offering no alternative revenue source [S3].
The bill contained no guardrails tying the tax cut to actual investment or hiring; the 'Job Creation' framing in the title was not backed by any such requirement in the text [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would flow almost entirely to the households with the largest investment gains, while the cost — lost federal revenue — would be spread across everyone who depends on or pays for government. There was no mechanism in the bill ensuring any job-creation benefit to offset that revenue loss. On balance the costs to the broader public outweighed the narrow benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee after referral, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Knollenberg introduced the bill on May 26, 2001, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
No other member cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Committee on Ways and Means took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 107th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the wealthy investors who would have benefited from a capital gains tax cut gained nothing, and the federal Treasury kept revenue that would otherwise have been forgone.

for.name: Rep. Joe Knollenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate the individual capital gains tax; it was his bill with no cosponsors

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or report — leaving the bill to expire

sides.party_line_note: The bill had zero cosponsors and never reached a vote, so no party position was ever recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Wealthy households and investors with capital assets
industries.note: The bill would have made profits from selling stocks, real estate, and businesses tax-free; capital gains are concentrated among the highest-income households, and the revenue cost would fall on the general budget. The bill never advanced, so no benefit was delivered.
A capital gains exclusion could have encouraged more asset trading and investment activity that brokerages and asset managers profit from. The bill died in committee, so no effect materialized.
